title: The Sick Muse
text:
My poor muse, alas! what is wrong with you this day?

Night visions people your vacant eyes,

And taking turns I see reflected in your complexion

Madness and panic, cold and taciturn.


Have the greenish succubus and the rosy imp

Poured fear into you, and love, from their urns?

With their fist did dark nightmares sink you

To the bottom of some fabulous Minturnae?


I would like that, exhaling a wholesome odor,

Your breast of strong ideas might be frequented

And your Christian blood might flow in rhythmic waves,


Like the multiple sounds of the ancient syllables

Where, in turn, Phoebus, father of song,

And great Pan, whose empire spreads through the harvests, reign.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the sick muse's nightmare imagery and the desired return of rhythmic, classical vitality.

title: To Théodore de Banville
text:
You seized the Goddess's thick hair

With such vigor that everyone would have taken you,

Seeing that haughty air and that beautiful abandon,

For a young ruffian striking his lover.


Your gaze set aflame by a precocious fire,

You displayed your craftsman's pride without shame

In those constructions whose correct audacity

Anticipates the fruits of your maturity.


Poet, our blood escapes through every pore.

Perhaps by chance the Centaur's garment,

Which transformed each vein into a funereal stream,


Was dyed three times in the subtle lavas

Of those monstrous, vengeful reptiles

That Hercules one day strangled in his cradle?
editorial_note: The translation keeps Baudelaire's violent compliment to Banville's craft and mythic imagery.

title: The Enemy
text:
My youth was nothing but a great storm

Crossed, in gusts, by blinding suns;

The winds and downpours wrought such havoc

That scarcely one ripe fruit remains in my garden.


I have reached the total autumn of thought,

And now it is necessary to use shovel and rake

To bring afloat the flooded lands

Where hollows opened, immense as tombs.


Who knows whether the new shoots I dream of

Will find in my soil, barren as a beach,

The mystic nourishment that would give them vigor?


—Oh grief! Oh grief! Time devours life,

And the dark enemy that gnaws our heart

Grows and strengthens on our own blood.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the storm-damaged garden and Time as the enemy feeding on the heart's blood.

title: Condemnation
text:
The inextricable and hard bank,

The arduous passage, the voracious maelstrom,

Drag less sand and less impure brushwood


Than our hearts, where the sky is seen;

They are like promontories in the serene air,

Where the lighthouse flashes, beneficent sentinel,

But below are mined by corrosive limpets;


We might compare them still to the lodging,

Hope of the hungry, where at night they knock,

Swearing, wounded, broken, asking asylum,

Prelates and students, whores and soldiers.


They will never return to the filthy bedrooms;

War, science, and love, nothing needs us.

The atrium was frozen, wine and bed infected;

One must serve such visitors on one's knees!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the source's difficult syntax and images of eroded hearts, asylum, and kneeling service.

title: Dream of a Curious Man
text:
You know, as in my case, that savory pain,

And make people say of you: "What a singular being!"

—I was about to die. And in my loving soul there was,

Desire mixed with horror, a rare suffering;


Anguish and hope, without discordant mood.

The more the ineluctable sand emptied,

The more delicious and harsh my torture became;

My soul was breaking away from the familiar world.


And I was like that child, greedy for spectacles,

Who hates the curtain as one hates a barrier.

Until, at last, the cold truth was unveiled:


Without feeling it, I had died, and the terrible dawn

Surrounded me. —What! Is this all, at last?

The curtain had risen and I was still waiting.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the death-as-theater conceit and the anticlimax after the curtain rises.
